title: Dear Workaholic Colleague
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing ahead of Thanksgiving break, Stuart makes a professional (not just personal) case for rest, grounding it in the Yerkes-Dodson performance-pressure curve and warning that teaching's high stakes plus dehumanizing systems push over-pressure toward being the default state. His sharper argument is about identity: teachers who let their job become their whole sense of self are set up to suffer either way, since both failure and success at teaching then get processed as verdicts on personal worth rather than as normal professional outcomes. He describes failure under this enmeshment as a "spiritual judgment" of inadequacy, and success as a kind of "spiritual cocaine" that inflates ego and demands ever more validation. Both patterns, he argues, cost a person their rootedness and sense of self. The piece ends with concrete, almost playful permission-giving: turn off email, leave the laptop at school, take a nap, play a board game — anything that reconnects a teacher with who they are outside the job.
points: Stuart frames rest as a professional competency on par with lesson design or classroom management, not a personal indulgence separate from the job.

He identifies job-identity enmeshment, not workload alone, as the deeper driver of burnout: both failure and success get processed as verdicts on personal worth when a teacher's identity and job title collapse into one thing.
The "spiritual cocaine" image for identity-driven success names a real risk of praise-seeking and ego inflation among high-performing, well-regarded teachers, not just struggling ones.
Practical rest guidance (turn off email, leave the laptop at school, take a nap) is offered as the concrete antidote, deliberately mundane rather than aspirational.
quotes: Human beings can only take so much pressure before their performance declines. Psychologists Yerkes and Dodson codified this idea over 100 years ago with what I call the Yerkes-Dodson Curve.
When you add the stakes to the dehumanizing nature of so many of our policies and systems, it's a mundane observation to say that over-pressure is the default.

A major cause of teacher attrition, by my observation, is when we as teachers allow our jobs to become our source of identity. If you can't look in the mirror and see more than a teacher, more than a person with all these job responsibilities and all these student problems to handle, you're on the path to burnout.

When an identity-enmeshed teacher fails, their whole soul writhes in agony. The bad day in the classroom becomes so much more than just that; it becomes an indictment of our human value, a spiritual judgment that we are lacking and inadequate as a human being.

On the other hand, when an identity-enmeshed teacher succeeds — when they win an award, when their students outperform the average on tests, when they get compliments in the grocery store from students or their parents — it is as if they've taken a hit of a spiritual cocaine.
In both cases, the end result is losing your sense of self, losing the kind of rootedness that is required for a flourishing life.
Thankfully, the best medicine for such dilemmas is often as simple as rest.
